stem: Select the sentence that points out what kind of comparison the biologists' evidence lacks.
explanation: This sentence names the flaw: the comparison is with the reef's own past, not with unprotected reefs. The final sentence then spells out the consequence.

answer.sentence: The conclusion is plausible, but it rests on a comparison with the reef's own condition before the ban, not on a comparison with unprotected reefs over the same decade.

stem: Which of the following does the author give as a reason to treat the result with caution?
explanation: The cautious reading cites observation effects ('knew they were being observed') and the firm's self-paced work.

choiceExplanations.A: The author never criticizes the length of the trial.
choiceExplanations.B: Nothing says employees disliked it; the passage says they valued it.
choiceExplanations.D: The hospital ward is a hypothetical setting; no result is reported.
choiceExplanations.E: The firm's size is never mentioned.

choices.text: Productivity was measured for only six months, which the author says is too short.
Employees disliked the four-day week.
Employees who knew they were observed may have worked harder than usual.
Productivity fell at a hospital ward that tried the schedule.
The firm was too large to be studied reliably.

stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the biologists' conclusion?
explanation: A parallel rise at unprotected reefs would supply the alternative explanation the author describes, undermining the credit given to the ban.

choiceExplanations.A: If anything, this supports the idea that fishing had suppressed the fish population.
choiceExplanations.B: The number of species does not bear on why the fish population grew.
choiceExplanations.C: Where boats go now does not show what caused the rise at this reef.
choiceExplanations.D: Larger fish do not show what caused the increase in numbers.

choices.text: Before the ban, the protected reef had been heavily overfished.
The protected reef contains more fish species than any other reef in the region.
Fishing boats from the island now work at other reefs.
Some fish on the protected reef have grown larger than before.
Over the same decade, fish numbers on nearby unprotected reefs also roughly tripled.

stem: Which of the following findings would most support the by-product explanation of dialects?
explanation: The by-product view predicts bigger differences where groups seldom exchange birds, so such a finding supports it.

choiceExplanations.A: This supports the first hypothesis, not the by-product view.
choiceExplanations.B: Density of populations is not related to copying errors accumulating in isolation.
choiceExplanations.D: This contradicts the by-product view, which predicts differences between isolated groups.
choiceExplanations.E: Variety among tutors does not show errors accumulating in isolation.

choices.text: In several species, females prefer the songs of local males.
Males sing more elaborate songs when populations are dense.
In a species whose young rarely change groups, neighboring populations' songs differ more than those of populations that exchange young birds often.
Isolated groups of birds sing songs that are indistinguishable from one another.
Adult tutors in one population sing a wider range of songs than those in another.

stem: Select the sentence that gives a reason for doubting the first hypothesis.
explanation: The mixed experimental results (some species show no preference) are the evidence against the hypothesis.

answer.sentence: Experiments, however, have produced mixed results: in some species, females prefer local songs, while in others, they show no preference.

stem: Consider each of the three answer choices separately and select all that apply. Which of the following conclusions would the author regard as reasonable on the basis of the trial?
explanation: The author's own last sentence supports A. B and C extend the result to settings beyond the trial, exactly what the author cautions against.

choiceExplanations.B: The author warns the result 'may not extend' to settings where output depends on presence.
choiceExplanations.C: The author names the call center as a place the result may not extend to.

choices.text: In at least one setting a long workweek was not needed to maintain productivity.
Long workweeks are largely wasted time in every kind of workplace.
A call center adopting the same schedule would lose no productivity.

stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's suggestion that income explains the observed association?
explanation: If the association persists among residents with similar incomes, income cannot be the whole explanation.

choiceExplanations.A: Lower crime is another possible explanation, but it does not show that income is not responsible.
choiceExplanations.C: Frequency of moving does not bear on whether income explains the health differences.
choiceExplanations.D: Even if everyone uses parks, income could still account for the difference in health.
choiceExplanations.E: Age is a separate factor and does not reduce the plausibility of income as an explanation.

choices.text: Greener neighborhoods tend to have lower crime rates.
Residents with similar incomes who live in greener neighborhoods report better health than those in barer ones.
Higher-income families move more often than lower-income families.
Parks are used by residents of all income levels.
Older residents are more likely to report good health.

stem: Consider each of the three answer choices separately and select all that apply. Which of the following criticisms of the conclusion that gut bacteria cause obesity does the author make?
explanation: A and B are the two stated limits. C contradicts the author's concession.

choiceExplanations.C: The author grants that the bacteria 'can influence weight gain under laboratory conditions'.

choices.text: Findings in laboratory mice may not carry over to people with varied diets, genes and microbial exposure.
The bacteria might be a consequence of eating habits linked to obesity rather than a cause.
The experiment shows that bacteria cannot influence weight at all.

stem: According to the passage, a study following people who move to greener areas for reasons unrelated to health would be informative mainly because it would
explanation: The problem identified is non-random selection into neighborhoods; moves for non-health reasons reduce that problem.

choiceExplanations.B: No study can 'guarantee' this; the point is reducing the role of self-selection.
choiceExplanations.C: The passage thinks green space may well contribute to health.
choiceExplanations.D: Stress is mentioned only as a proposed mechanism.

choices.text: help separate the effect of green space from the effect of which people choose to live there
guarantee that income no longer affects health
show that green space harms health
measure stress directly
make any comparison with other neighborhoods unnecessary

stem: Select the sentence that offers an alternative to the interpretation that gut bacteria cause obesity.
explanation: The alternative is that the bacteria are 'merely a consequence' of eating habits. The earlier objection concerns generalizing to people, not an alternative cause.

answer.sentence: Moreover, the experiment cannot reveal whether in free-living animals the bacteria are a cause of obesity or merely a consequence of the eating habits that accompany it.

stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the inference that a planet with a measured low density is rich in gas?
explanation: If low-density planets can be made of something other than gas, the step from low density to gas-rich is undermined.

choiceExplanations.A: Which stars the planets orbit does not bear on what low density indicates.
choiceExplanations.C: Larger size is consistent with, not a threat to, the inference.
choiceExplanations.D: This concerns the difficulty of measuring, not the link between density and composition.
choiceExplanations.E: Their rarity does not change what low density suggests.

choices.text: Most planets with low densities orbit faint stars.
Some planets made mostly of water or ice also have low densities.
Gas-rich planets are generally larger than rocky ones.
Spectral shifts are hard to measure for distant stars.
High-density planets are rare among known planets.

stem: Consider each of the three answer choices separately and select all that apply. A researcher proposes describing the typical composition of all known planets using only planets with measured densities. Which of the following points from the passage suggest caution?
explanation: The planets with measured densities skew away from faint or distant stars, so they may not represent all known planets: that calls for caution. Having been measured by two methods is irrelevant to representativeness, and the passage says nothing about the reliability of the measurements.

choiceExplanations.B: How many methods were used does not bear on representativeness.
choiceExplanations.C: The passage never says these measurements are less reliable.

choices.text: Planets around faint or distant stars are likely to be under-represented among them.
Such planets have been measured by two different methods.
Their measured densities are less reliable than other estimates.

stem: Select the sentence that gives a reason to doubt that the findings merely reflect workers' resistance to change.
explanation: The sentence reports the managers' objection and then answers it: the studies took place months after the move, long enough for novelty and irritation to fade.

answer.sentence: Some managers dismiss these findings as the product of workers' resistance to change, but the studies were carried out months after the move, long enough for novelty and irritation to have faded.

stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that in cold climates the winter penalty of a white roof can cancel its summer savings?
explanation: If snow covers the roof all winter, the color underneath makes little difference, so a white roof loses little winter warmth and the penalty could not cancel the summer savings. The alternatives strengthen the claim or address something else.

choiceExplanations.A: This is already stated in the passage and bears on pedestrians, not on heating bills.
choiceExplanations.C: A larger heating bill makes the winter penalty weigh more, which supports the claim.
choiceExplanations.D: This shrinks the summer savings, so it helps the claim rather than weakening it.
choiceExplanations.E: Purchase price is a different issue from the balance of heating and cooling costs.

choices.text: The cooling effect of white roofs at street level is small.
In cold climates, roofs are usually covered by snow throughout the heating season.
Heating a home in a cold climate costs more than cooling a home in a hot one.
Air conditioning is installed in few homes in cold climates.
White paint costs more than dark paint.

stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that clients' ability to retaliate keeps cleaners honest?
explanation: If cleaners are equally honest whether or not clients punish them, punishment cannot be what keeps them honest. The other options are on the topic but do not touch the link between retaliation and honesty.

choiceExplanations.A: A fact about location with no bearing on the claim.
choiceExplanations.B: The passage already says this; it explains the temptation to cheat, not the effect of retaliation.
choiceExplanations.C: Nothing here bears on whether retaliation affects the cleaners' behavior.
choiceExplanations.E: Size is unrelated to whether the threat of retaliation keeps cleaners honest.

choices.text: Cleaning stations are found mostly in warm, shallow water.
Mucus is more nutritious to cleaners than parasites are.
Some clients visit more than one cleaning station.
Cleaners at stations where clients seldom chase them are just as honest as cleaners at stations where clients chase them often.
Cleaners that bite mucus are, on average, larger than those that do not.

stem: Consider each of the three answer choices separately and select all that apply. Which of the following, if true, would weaken the author's judgment that noise-based imaging 'deserves serious attention'?
explanation: The second choice casts doubt on the method's reliability. The third means the evenly spread sources the method needs would rarely exist. Existing stations make the method cheaper, which strengthens the author's view.

choiceExplanations.A: This lowers the cost of using the method, so it supports the author's judgment.

choices.text: Many seismic stations that could record ocean noise are already installed.
Structures reconstructed from ocean noise have repeatedly disagreed with those found by other methods in the same region.
In most regions, ocean noise is dominated year-round by a few intense, localized sources.

stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's suggestion that these associations may fade as migrants disperse into cities?
explanation: The author's reasoning is that dispersal weakens the ties that enforce reputation. If dispersed migrants still pass news of defaults quickly, the enforcement survives and the associations need not fade.

choiceExplanations.A: This fits the claim that reputation works in close-knit places and says nothing about cities.
choiceExplanations.B: Where associations are found does not bear on whether dispersal weakens them.
choiceExplanations.C: This would support the suggestion that the associations fade.
choiceExplanations.D: Already part of the description; irrelevant to dispersal.

choices.text: Defaults in village-based associations are extremely rare.
Economists have documented such associations on several continents.
Reputation matters less to residents of large cities than to villagers.
Most such associations require every member to contribute the same sum each month.
Migrants who disperse across a city generally stay in touch through networks that quickly spread news of any member's default.

stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's view that the more dramatic claims about fungal networks have outrun the evidence?
explanation: The author says that the missing evidence is whether connected seedlings do better. A field experiment showing they do would fill that gap and weaken the view. The other options are granted facts, irrelevant, or supportive of the author.

choiceExplanations.B: Also granted; the gap is between transfer and benefit.
choiceExplanations.C: This fits the author's suggestion that fungi act for their own ends, so it would strengthen rather than weaken the view.
choiceExplanations.D: A fact about cost, irrelevant to the strength of the evidence.
choiceExplanations.E: Already granted in the passage; it does not show that the transfers benefit trees.

choices.text: A field experiment found that seedlings joined to a mature tree by fungi survive at markedly higher rates than comparable unconnected seedlings.
Carbon supplied to one tree has been found in the tissues of its neighbors.
Fungi receive sugars from the trees whose roots they colonize.
Greenhouse experiments cost less than field experiments.
Fungi colonize the roots of most species of trees.

stem: Consider each of the three answer choices separately and select all that apply. Which of the following, if true, would weaken the author's claim that the entries in which the landless poor appear can reveal what the authorities feared or tolerated?
explanation: If the entries follow fixed forms, or the prosecutions were random, they would not reflect what authorities feared or tolerated. Illiteracy explains the thin record but leaves the claim untouched.

choiceExplanations.B: This explains why they left few records but does not affect whether the entries that exist reveal the authorities' concerns.

choices.text: Authorities brought the landless poor to court at random, without regard to any particular fear or concern.
Many landless people could not sign their names.
Entries about landless defendants were copied from standard forms that did not vary with any concern of the authorities.

stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the inference that free evenings mainly attract people who would have visited anyway?
explanation: If the surveyed group was skewed toward early arrivals who differ from later ones, the survey's finding may not describe free-evening visitors as a whole. The other options leave the inference intact.

choiceExplanations.B: The passage already says attendance is impressive; this says nothing about who attends.
choiceExplanations.C: This bears on the author's suggestion about outreach, not on the inference from the survey.
choiceExplanations.D: This does not show that the surveyed sample misrepresents free-evening visitors.
choiceExplanations.E: A scheduling detail that says nothing about who the visitors are or whether the sample is fair.

choices.text: The survey was handed out only during the first hour of free evenings, and visitors arriving later were disproportionately from lower-income households.
Attendance on free evenings is higher than on paying days.
Outreach programs in other cities have raised attendance among infrequent visitors.
The museum's paying visitors have even higher incomes than its free-evening visitors.
The free evening is held on the same weekday each week.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the council's conclusion that free parking revived the commerce of the central shopping street?
explanation: The council infers cause from timing: receipts rose faster after the meters went. A new rail link opening in the same period offers another explanation for the extra shoppers, so the rise need not be due to free parking.

choiceExplanations.A: A decline at the malls fits the council's story that shoppers are returning to the street; it does not weaken it.
choiceExplanations.B: What some owners thought beforehand says nothing about what caused the later rise in receipts.
choiceExplanations.D: Lost meter revenue is a cost of the policy, not evidence about whether it revived commerce.
choiceExplanations.E: This bears on the proposal for other districts, not on the conclusion drawn about the central street.

choices.text: Over the past two years, sales tax receipts at the suburban malls have declined slightly.
Several shop owners on the central street opposed the removal of the meters when it was first proposed.
A few months after the meters were removed, a light-rail station opened at one end of the street, giving it its first direct rail link to the city's residential suburbs.
Before their removal, the meters on the central street had produced a substantial share of the city's parking revenue.
The three districts in which the council now proposes to remove meters contain fewer retail businesses than the central street does.

stem: The council's conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
explanation: The argument treats the gap between 18 and 6 percent as the effect of free parking. That works only if the gap would not have appeared without the change; if it would have, the comparison shows nothing about the meters.

choiceExplanations.A: Free parking could matter even if only a minority of shoppers drive, so the argument does not need a majority.
choiceExplanations.B: This concerns the proposal for other districts, and it is far stronger than anything the conclusion about the central street requires.
choiceExplanations.C: The street's commerce could revive without any loss at the malls, so this is not required.
choiceExplanations.E: The receipts have already risen; the argument does not need to rule out a deterrent effect that the figures suggest was outweighed.

choices.text: Most of the shoppers who visit the central street arrive there by car.
Removing the meters from the three other districts will raise their receipts by as much as the central street's rose.
Since the meters were removed, sales tax receipts at the suburban malls have fallen.
Had the meters remained, the street's receipts would not have grown substantially faster than those of the rest of the city anyway.
Shoppers are not deterred by the commuters who now occupy the free spaces for most of the day.

stem: In the passage, the critics' objection about the occupied spaces functions primarily as
explanation: The council does not deny that commuters fill the spaces; it replies that the sales figures speak for themselves, setting the objection aside rather than refuting it.

choiceExplanations.A: The council does not cite the objection; the critics raise it against the policy.
choiceExplanations.C: All-day occupation by commuters is offered as a drawback of the policy, not as a cause of higher receipts.
choiceExplanations.D: The passage reports the council's conclusion and the critics' objection; the objection is not its main point.
choiceExplanations.E: The council concedes nothing about the figures; it relies on them.

choices.text: evidence the council cites in support of extending its policy to other districts
a concern that the council answers not by disputing it but by appealing to other evidence
an alternative explanation for the faster growth of the street's sales tax receipts
the main conclusion that the passage as a whole is meant to establish
a fact that the council concedes calls the reliability of the sales figures into question

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the managers' conclusion that predation by mink caused the declines in the tern colonies?
explanation: The managers rely on a correlation between mink and declining colonies. If the islands the mink reached also lost their food supply at the same time, the declines can be explained without predation.

choiceExplanations.A: What else mink eat does not bear on whether they caused the tern declines.
choiceExplanations.B: Physical evidence of mink attacks on nests supports the managers' conclusion.
choiceExplanations.C: Results elsewhere concern how well trapping works, not what caused the declines.
choiceExplanations.D: When the mink arrived in the region says nothing about whether they or something else reduced the colonies.

choices.text: Mink also take the eggs of several species of duck that nest on the islands.
On the islands the mink reached, many destroyed tern nests showed tooth marks characteristic of mink.
Trapping programs on other coasts have reduced the number of mink without eliminating the animals.
Mink were first brought to the region's fur farms several decades before they reached the islands.
The islands the mink reached are those nearest the mainland, where in the 1990s commercial fishing sharply depleted the small fish that terns feed to their chicks.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most strongly supports the managers' explanation of why tern numbers have recovered only partially?
explanation: If terns return to breed where they were raised, sites where some birds kept breeding would keep producing returning recruits, while sites abandoned entirely would draw few. Recovery that is fastest exactly where breeding never stopped fits that explanation.

choiceExplanations.B: Birds readily settling on islands where they were not raised would contradict the claimed habit, weakening the explanation.
choiceExplanations.C: Surviving mink offer a rival explanation for the slow recovery, so this weakens the managers' account.
choiceExplanations.D: Growth on islands the mink never reached does not show why the cleared islands recover slowly.
choiceExplanations.E: Different removal dates might explain differences between islands, but they lend no support to the homing explanation in particular.

choices.text: On the cleared islands, the colonies that have recovered most fully are those at which a few pairs continued to breed throughout the years when mink were present.
Young terns raised on islands the mink never reached frequently settle to breed on islands from which mink have been removed.
A small number of mink have evaded trapping on several of the cleared islands and continue to raid nests.
Tern colonies on islands the mink never reached have grown slightly since trapping began.
Mink were removed from the different islands at different times over the course of the decade.

stem: Consider each of the three choices separately and select all that apply. Which of the following can be properly inferred from the passage?
explanation: Tern numbers on the islands cleared of mink have recovered only partially, so clearing alone has not restored them. The managers explain the shortfall by the terns' habit of returning to breed where they were raised, an explanation that involves no surviving mink.

choiceExplanations.B: The passage says these colonies held steady during the 1990s; it gives no information about any change since trapping began.

choices.text: Removing mink from an island has not by itself been enough to bring tern numbers there back to their earlier levels.
Tern colonies on the islands the mink never reached have grown since trapping began.
The managers' explanation of the incomplete recovery does not depend on any mink remaining on the cleared islands.

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the researchers' conclusion?
explanation: The comparison is meant to isolate labeling as the only difference between the two sets of outlets. A new, heavily advertised low-calorie line offered only in the first province is a second difference that could explain the drop.

choiceExplanations.A: Outlet size has no evident bearing on the calorie content of what diners order.
choiceExplanations.C: Similar starting points make the comparison fairer, so this strengthens rather than weakens the conclusion.
choiceExplanations.D: The study used the chain's outlets, and slow compliance elsewhere would if anything hide an effect, not create one.
choiceExplanations.E: This bears on how much the neighboring province might benefit, not on whether labeling caused the decline.

choices.text: The chain's outlets in the neighboring province are, on average, larger than its outlets in the first province.
During the year after the requirement took effect, the chain introduced a line of reduced-calorie dishes at its outlets in the first province only and advertised them heavily there.
Before the requirement took effect, the average calorie content of meals ordered at the chain's outlets was about the same in the two provinces.
Some independent restaurants in the first province were slow to comply with the requirement.
Diet-related illness is more common in the neighboring province than in the first province.

stem: Consider each of the three choices separately and select all that apply. Which of the following, if true, would strengthen the researchers' conclusion?
explanation: The first choice ties the decline to the information the labels supplied, which is just what the conclusion claims. The second rules out other differences between the two groups of outlets. The third places the decline before any labels appeared, so it weakens the conclusion.

choiceExplanations.C: A decline that came before the labels were printed cannot have been caused by them; it points to publicity instead.

choices.text: In the first province, the decline was concentrated in dishes whose printed calorie counts were much higher than most diners had guessed.
Throughout the study period, the chain's menus, prices and promotions were identical in the two provinces.
Most of the decline in the first province occurred during the months of public debate before the requirement took effect.

stem: In the researchers' argument, the chain's outlets in the neighboring province serve primarily to
explanation: Without the second group, a drop in the first province could reflect a chain-wide trend. Unchanged figures in the neighboring province suggest that the drop was specific to the province with labels.

choiceExplanations.A: The neighboring province had no labels at all, so its outlets cannot show anything about how labels work there.
choiceExplanations.B: The effect is measured in the first province; the other outlets serve as a baseline, not an illustration.
choiceExplanations.C: Nothing about the outlets bears on whether the province could adopt the rule.
choiceExplanations.D: Calorie content was unchanged in the neighboring province; this says nothing about a preference for lighter meals.

choices.text: show that calorie labeling is ineffective where diners are unfamiliar with it
illustrate the effect that the labeling requirement had on diners in the first province
demonstrate that the neighboring province is able to adopt the same rule
establish that diners in both provinces prefer lighter meals
indicate whether the decline in the first province reflected a change occurring throughout the chain

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the inference that the settlement carried on regular trade with the southern workshops?
explanation: The trade inference assumes the pottery was made in the south. Local clay means the pieces were made near the hilltop, which removes the reason to posit trade with the southern workshops.

choiceExplanations.B: Northern pottery at the southern workshops points to contact between the two places, which supports trade.
choiceExplanations.C: A kiln built after the pottery first appears weakens the case for local manufacture, which if anything helps the trade view.
choiceExplanations.D: Finds along the route between the regions fit the idea that goods moved from south to north.
choiceExplanations.E: What else the southern workshops made does not bear on where the hilltop's painted ware came from.

choices.text: Chemical analysis shows that the clay of the painted fragments comes from a deposit a few kilometers from the hilltop and matches no clay source in the south.
Fragments of pottery made at the hilltop settlement have been found at the southern workshops.
The kiln at the settlement was built several generations after painted pottery first appears there.
Pottery in the southern style has been found at a number of sites along the river between the two regions.
The southern workshops produced coarse cooking ware as well as painted pottery.

stem: Which of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the claim that the painted pottery was made at the settlement?
explanation: Wasters are discarded where firing fails, so finding them among the painted fragments would point to firing on site, and their absence would favor import. The answer bears directly on the claim of local manufacture.

choiceExplanations.A: Exports to other places say nothing about whether this settlement's painted ware was imported or made there.
choiceExplanations.B: Population size does not indicate where the painted pottery was made.
choiceExplanations.C: The size of the southern workshops does not bear on whether this pottery came from them.
choiceExplanations.E: The use of the coarse ware does not tell us whether the painted ware was produced locally.

choices.text: Whether the southern workshops also sent pottery to settlements east of them
Approximately how many people lived at the hilltop settlement
Whether the southern workshops were larger than workshops in other regions of the period
Whether the painted fragments include wasters, pieces cracked or warped in firing that were seldom carried far from where they were fired
Whether the coarse ware from the kiln was used for cooking or for storage

stem: The final sentence of the passage primarily serves to
explanation: The local-production view rests on the southern-style kiln. The last sentence notes that the kiln yielded only coarse ware and that no painting tools were found, which weakens the link between that kiln and the painted pottery.

choiceExplanations.A: The sentence works against local production, not for it.
choiceExplanations.B: Weakening one piece of evidence for local production does not prove the trade view; 'conclusively' overstates the sentence's role.
choiceExplanations.D: The sentence does not dispute the kiln's design, only what was fired in it.
choiceExplanations.E: Coarse cooking ware was apparently fired in the kiln, so some pottery was made at the settlement.

choices.text: support the view that the painted pottery was made at the settlement
establish conclusively that the painted pottery reached the settlement through trade
cast doubt on the relevance of the evidence offered by those who hold that the painted pottery was made on site
suggest that the kiln was not, in fact, built to a southern design
indicate that no pottery of any kind was produced at the settlement

stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the climatologists' interpretation of the increase in lightning strikes?
explanation: The climatologists read more strikes as a sign of more unstable air. If more particles make each storm produce more lightning, the count could rise even if the air is no more unstable than before.

choiceExplanations.A: Rising temperatures fit the claim that warming is at work, so this supports rather than weakens it.
choiceExplanations.B: More lightning fires confirm that lightning increased; they do not challenge the explanation for the increase.
choiceExplanations.C: The climatologists already rely on counts from the original sensors alone, so where the new ones stand does not undercut that reply.
choiceExplanations.D: Similar increases elsewhere are consistent with a broad warming effect and do not count against it.

choices.text: Average summer temperatures in the region rose by more than a degree between 1990 and 2020.
Forest fires started by lightning have become more frequent in the region since 1990.
Most of the newer sensors were installed in remote areas far from the original ones.
Several regions farther south have recorded comparable increases in lightning over the same period.

Since 1990, smoke and industrial particles carried into the region each summer have increased sharply, and such particles are known to multiply the strikes a storm produces without making storms more frequent.

stem: The climatologists' reply in the final sentence depends on which of the following assumptions?
explanation: The reply uses the original sensors as a constant instrument. If those sensors had themselves become more sensitive, their rising counts could reflect better detection rather than more lightning.

choiceExplanations.A: The reply concerns only the original sensors; how many strikes the newer ones recorded is beside the point.
choiceExplanations.C: The reply needs only that the increase is real, not that warming is the sole possible cause; 'only' is far too strong.
choiceExplanations.D: An uneven spread of strikes would not matter as long as the same sensors detected them in the same way over time.
choiceExplanations.E: Future expansion has no bearing on whether the past counts are comparable.

choices.text: The newer sensors recorded more strikes in total than the original sensors did.
The original sensors did not become more sensitive to faint or distant strikes over the period.
Warming is the only factor that can make the region's summer air more unstable.
Lightning strikes were evenly distributed across the area that the original sensors cover.
The sensor network will not be expanded again in the coming decades.

stem: It can be inferred from the passage that
explanation: The climatologists concede that the increase is smaller when only the original sensors are counted. So some of the full increase comes from the added sensors detecting strikes the original ones missed.

choiceExplanations.B: The climatologists say the increase persists among the original sensors, so this contradicts the passage.
choiceExplanations.C: The passage reports the climatologists' view and an objection to it; nothing establishes warming as the sole cause.
choiceExplanations.D: The newer sensors detect strikes the older ones missed, which is not a sign of lower reliability.
choiceExplanations.E: The passage gives no information about the intensity of storms.

choices.text: at least part of the recorded increase in lightning strikes reflects additions to the sensor network rather than a change in the weather
the original sensors recorded no increase in lightning strikes between 1990 and 2020
warming is the sole cause of the increase in lightning strikes in the region
the newer sensors are less reliable than the original ones
thunderstorms in the region have become less intense since 1990
